title: Building Interactive Apps with Shiny
text: A practical lecture note for analysts ready to move beyond static reports

title: Building Interactive Apps with Shiny
text:
What is Shiny?
If you’ve ever finished an R analysis and thought “I wish my manager could just drag a slider and see this update” — that’s exactly what Shiny solves.
Shiny is an R package developed by Posit (formerly RStudio) that lets you turn ordinary R code into a fully interactive web application — without writing a single line of JavaScript, HTML, or CSS (unless you want to). Your colleague can open a URL in a browser, adjust inputs, and see outputs update in real time, all powered by R running on a server behind the scenes.






NoteThe core idea in one sentence



Shiny wraps R in a reactive framework: when an input changes (a slider, a dropdown, a text box), any output that depends on it automatically re-runs and updates.

title: Building Interactive Apps with Shiny
text:
The Two-Part Structure
Every Shiny app has exactly two logical pieces:








Part
What it does
Where it lives




UI (ui)
Defines the layout and controls the user sees
ui.R or the ui object


Server (server)
Contains the R code that produces outputs
server.R or the server function



You can write these in two separate files (ui.R + server.R) or in a single app.R file. For learning purposes, a single file is easiest.

title: Building Interactive Apps with Shiny
Building Interactive Apps with Shiny
text:
Understanding Reactivity
Reactivity is what makes Shiny feel alive. The rule is simple:

Any output that reads input$x will automatically re-run whenever input$x changes.

You don’t call a refresh function. You don’t write event listeners. Shiny tracks the dependency for you.

The reactive graph
[sliderInput: n]  ──────►  [renderText: result]
If you had two outputs both reading input$n, they would both re-run when the slider moves. If you had an output that reads input$a and input$b, it re-runs when either changes.


reactive() — sharing computed values
If multiple outputs need the same intermediate computation, don’t repeat the code. Wrap it in reactive():

server <- function(input, output) {
  
  # Computed once, shared by multiple outputs
  filtered_data <- reactive({
    mtcars[mtcars$cyl == input$cyl, ]
  })
  
  output$plot  <- renderPlot({ plot(filtered_data()$wt, filtered_data()$mpg) })
  output$table <- renderTable({ filtered_data() })
}

Note: you call a reactive expression like a function — filtered_data() — with parentheses.

title: Building Interactive Apps with Shiny
text:
Key UI Components
Shiny has built-in input and output widgets for almost everything you need.

Inputs

# Numeric input
sliderInput("year", "Select year:", min = 2018, max = 2024, value = 2022)

# Dropdown
selectInput("channel", "Channel:", choices = c("Mobile", "Paid Search", "Affiliate", "Social Media"))

# Checkbox group
checkboxGroupInput("methods", "Attribution methods:",
                   choices = c("First Touch", "Last Touch", "Markov"),
                   selected = "Markov")

# Date range
dateRangeInput("dates", "Date range:",
               start = "2024-01-01", end = Sys.Date())



Outputs

# In the UI: declare where each output goes
plotOutput("my_chart")
tableOutput("my_table")
textOutput("my_text")
verbatimTextOutput("my_code_output")

# In the server: produce each output
output$my_chart <- renderPlot({ ... })
output$my_table <- renderTable({ ... })
output$my_text  <- renderText({ ... })

title: Building Interactive Apps with Shiny
section: A More Realistic Example: Attribution Explorer
text:
A More Realistic Example: Attribution Explorer
Here is a Shiny app closer to something you might actually use — an interactive attribution comparison tool:

library(shiny)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# Data
attr_data <- data.frame(
  channel = rep(c("Mobile", "Paid Search", "Affiliate", "Social Media"), 3),
  method  = rep(c("First Touch", "Last Touch", "Markov"), each = 4),
  credits = c(21, 34, 17, 10,   # first touch
              26, 15, 18, 8,    # last touch
              21, 20, 20, 21)   # markov
)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Attribution Model Explorer"),
  
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      checkboxGroupInput(
        "methods",
        "Select attribution models:",
        choices  = unique(attr_data$method),
        selected = unique(attr_data$method)
      ),
      hr(),
      p("Adjust which models to display and compare how each model assigns
        credit to the four marketing channels.")
    ),
    
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("attr_chart", height = "400px"),
      hr(),
      tableOutput("attr_table")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output) {
  
  filtered <- reactive({
    attr_data |> filter(method %in% input$methods)
  })
  
  output$attr_chart <- renderPlot({
    ggplot(filtered(), aes(x = channel, y = credits, fill = method)) +
      geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.65) +
      scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
      labs(title = "Conversion Credits by Channel and Model",
           x = NULL, y = "Credits", fill = "Model") +
      theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
  })
  
  output$attr_table <- renderTable({
    filtered() |>
      tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = method, values_from = credits)
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)

title: Building Interactive Apps with Shiny
text:
Layout Options
Shiny gives you several layout options to structure more complex apps.

sidebarLayout() — most common
Controls on the left, output on the right. Used in the example above.


navbarPage() — multi-tab apps

ui <- navbarPage(
  "My App",
  tabPanel("Overview",   plotOutput("overview_plot")),
  tabPanel("Data Table", tableOutput("data_table")),
  tabPanel("About",      p("This app was built with Shiny."))
)



fluidRow() + column() — custom grids

ui <- fluidPage(
  fluidRow(
    column(4, wellPanel(sliderInput(...))),
    column(8, plotOutput("chart"))
  )
)

title: Building Interactive Apps with Shiny
section: How to Deploy a Shiny App
text:
How to Deploy a Shiny App
A Shiny app requires a live R process to run. That means you can’t just put the files on a web server like a static HTML page — you need somewhere R is actually executing.









Option
Cost
Difficulty
Best for




shinyapps.io (Posit)
Free tier available
Easy
Sharing with anyone


Posit Connect
Paid (org license)
Medium
Internal enterprise use


Shiny Server (self-hosted)
Free (server cost)
Hard
Full control


Docker + cloud
Pay-as-you-go
Hard
Production scale



For class and portfolio purposes, shinyapps.io is the easiest path:

# Install rsconnect and deploy
install.packages("rsconnect")
library(rsconnect)

# Authenticate once (get token from shinyapps.io)
rsconnect::setAccountInfo(name = "YOUR_ACCOUNT",
                          token = "YOUR_TOKEN",
                          secret = "YOUR_SECRET")

# Deploy
rsconnect::deployApp(appDir = "path/to/your/app/")

title: Building Interactive Apps with Shiny
section: Common Mistakes (and How to Fix Them)
text:
Common Mistakes (and How to Fix Them)






WarningMistake 1: Forgetting parentheses on reactive expressions



filtered_data is a function — you must call it as filtered_data().








WarningMistake 2: Putting heavy computation outside reactive()



Code at the top level of server runs once at startup. If you need something to re-run when inputs change, it must be inside reactive(), renderPlot(), etc.








WarningMistake 3: Using input$x outside a reactive context



You can only read input values inside reactive(), render*(), or observe(). Reading input$x directly in a regular function will throw an error.

title: Building Interactive Apps with Shiny
text:
Summary
Shiny lets you go from an R script to a shareable, interactive web app without leaving R. The mental model is:

UI describes what the user sees and interacts with.
Server contains the R logic that produces outputs.
Reactivity connects them automatically — change an input, outputs update.

For analysts already comfortable in R and ggplot2, Shiny is a natural next step. The learning curve is mostly about understanding reactivity, not about R itself.






NoteWhat comes next?



In the next essay, we look at Shinylive — a way to run Shiny apps entirely in the browser, with no server required.

title: Shinylive: Serverless Shiny in the Browser
text: How WebAssembly makes it possible to run R in your browser — and why that changes everything

title: Shinylive: Serverless Shiny in the Browser
text:
The Traditional Problem
Every Shiny app you’ve built so far has a fundamental constraint: it needs a live R process running somewhere. When a user moves a slider, their browser sends a message to that R process, R re-runs the relevant code, and the result travels back. The browser is just a display terminal.
This is powerful — it means the full power of R and all its packages is available — but it creates friction:

You need a server (your own laptop, shinyapps.io, Posit Connect…)
Someone has to pay for that server
The app goes offline if the server does
Sharing becomes a deployment problem, not just a files problem

Shinylive solves this by making the server disappear entirely.

title: Shinylive: Serverless Shiny in the Browser
text:
What is Shinylive?
Shinylive is a version of Shiny that runs entirely inside the user’s web browser using WebAssembly (Wasm). There is no R server. R itself — the interpreter, the packages, everything — runs locally in the browser using a technology called webR.






NoteWebAssembly in plain language



WebAssembly is a low-level binary format that modern browsers can execute at near-native speed. Originally designed for C and C++ programs, it has been extended to run other languages — including R. The R interpreter has been compiled to Wasm and is distributed as a downloadable bundle. When a Shinylive app loads in your browser, it downloads that R bundle and starts executing your app code directly.


The result: a Shiny app that lives as a collection of static files (HTML, CSS, JS, Wasm blobs). You can host it on GitHub Pages, Netlify, any CDN — anywhere that can serve static files. No R process, no server management.

title: Shinylive: Serverless Shiny in the Browser
text:
How Shinylive Works Architecturally
Here is a side-by-side comparison of the two architectures:

Traditional Shiny
User browser  ──── HTTP request ────►  R Server
              ◄── rendered output ───  (Shiny running in R process)
                                       (input → reactive graph → output)
The browser is a thin client. All computation happens server-side.


Shinylive
User browser  ──── loads static files ────►  CDN / GitHub Pages / Netlify
              ◄──── HTML + JS + Wasm ──────  (no R process exists)
              
              [Browser now contains webR + your app code]
              [input → reactive graph → output all happen locally]
The browser is the entire compute environment. The CDN just serves files.

title: Shinylive: Serverless Shiny in the Browser
text:
Setting Up Shinylive in Quarto
You don’t need to install a separate package to use Shinylive in a Quarto document — you use the shinylive Quarto extension.

Step 1: Install the extension
# Run in your terminal from your project folder
quarto add quarto-ext/shinylive
This adds an _extensions/ folder to your project.


Step 2: Add the filter to your YAML
---
title: "My Shinylive Document"
format: html
filters:
  - shinylive
---


Step 3: Write a {shinylive-r} code block
```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  sliderInput("n", "Number", 1, 100, 50),
  textOutput("result")
)

server <- function(input, output) {
  output$result <- renderText(paste("Value:", input$n))
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```
When Quarto renders this document, it packages the app code and the webR runtime together. The resulting HTML file is fully self-contained — the Shiny app runs when anyone opens it.

title: Shinylive: Serverless Shiny in the Browser
text:
A Realistic Shinylive Example
Here is a more complete example of a Shinylive app embedded in a Quarto document. This could sit in one of your dashboard or report pages and work for any reader without any server:
```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 500

library(shiny)
library(ggplot2)

channels <- c("Mobile", "Paid Search", "Affiliate", "Social Media")

attr_df <- data.frame(
  channel = rep(channels, 3),
  model   = rep(c("First Touch", "Last Touch", "Markov"), each = 4),
  credits = c(21, 34, 17, 10,
              26, 15, 18,  8,
              21, 20, 20, 21)
)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Interactive Attribution Explorer"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      checkboxGroupInput("models", "Show models:",
                         choices  = unique(attr_df$model),
                         selected = unique(attr_df$model))
    ),
    mainPanel(plotOutput("p"))
  )
)

server <- function(input, output) {
  output$p <- renderPlot({
    sub <- attr_df[attr_df$model %in% input$models, ]
    ggplot(sub, aes(channel, credits, fill = model)) +
      geom_col(position = "dodge") +
      theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
      labs(x = NULL, y = "Credits", fill = NULL)
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```






TipThe standalone: true option



This tells Shinylive that the code block contains a complete, self-contained app (with its own shinyApp() call), rather than just a fragment. Always include this for full apps.

section: Shinylive vs Traditional Shiny: Full Comparison
text:
Shinylive vs Traditional Shiny: Full Comparison



Dimension
Traditional Shiny
Shinylive




Where R runs
Server (your machine, shinyapps.io, Posit Connect)
User's browser (via WebAssembly)


Hosting requirement
Live R process required
Any static file host (GitHub Pages, Netlify, CDN)


Cost to host
Free tier limited; paid plans for scale
Free (static hosting is cheap or free)


Initial load time
Fast (server already has R)
Slower — browser must download webR runtime (~5–20 MB)


Computation speed
Fast (server-grade hardware)
Slower (WebAssembly has overhead vs native)


Data privacy
Data sent to server (must secure server)
Data never leaves the browser ✓


Package support
Any CRAN package
Only packages compiled for Wasm (growing list)


Database connections
Full support (server can connect to any DB)
Not supported (no network sockets in Wasm)


File system access
Full server file system
Sandboxed virtual file system only


Scaling
Requires server scaling / load balancing
Infinite scale (each user runs their own instance)


Offline use
No (requires server connection)
Possible after initial load (assets can be cached)


Best for
Production apps, large data, DB connections
Educational content, portfolios, reports, prototypes

title: Shinylive: Serverless Shiny in the Browser
text:
Strengths of Shinylive

1. Zero infrastructure cost
Because Shinylive apps are static files, you can host them on GitHub Pages for free. There is no shinyapps.io monthly plan, no Posit Connect license, no server to maintain. For a student portfolio or teaching materials, this is a significant advantage.


2. Perfect for embedding in Quarto documents
Shinylive is deeply integrated with Quarto. A single .qmd file can contain text, code, plots, and live interactive Shiny widgets — all rendering to a single static HTML file. This makes it ideal for lecture notes, tutorials, and reproducible reports that need interactivity.


3. Data privacy by design
Because all computation happens locally in the browser, sensitive data never travels across the network to a server. For healthcare, government, or financial applications where data privacy is paramount, this is a structural advantage.


4. Infinite scale
Every user runs their own isolated R instance in their own browser tab. There is no shared server, so ten users or ten thousand users make no difference to the host.

title: Shinylive: Serverless Shiny in the Browser
text:
Weaknesses of Shinylive

1. Slow initial load
The first time a user opens a Shinylive app, their browser must download the webR runtime — roughly 5–20 MB depending on which packages are needed. On a fast connection this takes a few seconds; on a slow one it can feel sluggish. Traditional Shiny apps load almost instantly because R is already running on the server.


2. Limited package support
Not every R package can run in WebAssembly. Packages that depend on compiled C or Fortran code need to be specifically recompiled for Wasm. Posit maintains a growing list of supported packages, and popular ones like ggplot2, dplyr, and tidyr work — but if your app depends on a niche package, it may not be available yet.


3. No server-side resources
Traditional Shiny can connect to databases, read large files from disk, call external APIs, or run long-running background jobs. Shinylive can’t do any of this — WebAssembly runs in a sandboxed environment without access to network sockets or the host file system.


4. Slower computation
WebAssembly executes at roughly 50–80% of native speed for CPU-bound work. For simple interactive dashboards this is imperceptible, but for computationally heavy tasks (large matrix operations, bootstrap simulations, complex model fitting), the overhead becomes noticeable.

title: Shinylive: Serverless Shiny in the Browser
text:
When to Choose Which






TipQuick decision guide



Choose Shinylive when: - You’re embedding interactivity in a Quarto report or teaching document - You want to host on GitHub Pages or Netlify for free - Your app uses common packages (ggplot2, dplyr, shiny) - Data is small and privacy matters - You want to share with anyone, no logins
Choose Traditional Shiny when: - Your app connects to a database or reads large files - You need packages not yet available in webR - Your computation is heavy (fitting models, large data transformations) - You need production-grade uptime and monitoring - Your organization already has Posit Connect

title: Shinylive: Serverless Shiny in the Browser
section: The Bigger Picture: WebAssembly in Data Science
text:
The Bigger Picture: WebAssembly in Data Science
Shinylive is part of a broader trend: moving data science tools to the browser using WebAssembly. Pyodide brings Python to the browser the same way webR does for R. Observable’s Observable Plot and DuckDB-Wasm let you query millions of rows of data entirely client-side.
The trajectory is clear: increasingly, analytical work that once required a server will be executable locally. This changes how we think about sharing analyses — instead of spinning up infrastructure, we publish a URL.
For now, Shinylive sits at the intersection of these two worlds: it lowers the barrier to sharing interactive R work dramatically, at the cost of some performance and package coverage. As webR matures and more packages get compiled for Wasm, those limitations will shrink.

title: Shinylive: Serverless Shiny in the Browser
text:
Summary









Traditional Shiny
Shinylive




Core idea
R on a server, browser as display
R in the browser via WebAssembly


Best use case
Production apps, big data, DB
Portfolios, teaching, reports


Hosting
Needs live R process
Any static host


Packages
All of CRAN
Wasm-compiled subset


Privacy
Data goes to server
Data stays in browser



Shinylive is not a replacement for traditional Shiny — it’s a complement. Together, they cover the full spectrum from quick embeddable widgets to production enterprise applications, all within the same familiar R and Shiny programming model.
